history.q: Whose nearly intact tomb did Howard Carter discover in the Valley of the Kings in 1922?
history.fact: Tomb KV62 held more than 5,000 objects, including the famous gold funerary mask.

history.q: Which Macedonian conqueror founded the city of Alexandria in 331 BCE?
history.fact: Alexandria's Pharos lighthouse was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, and its Great Library became a legendary centre of learning.

history.q: Who was the last active ruler of Egypt's Ptolemaic Kingdom before it became a Roman province in 30 BCE?
history.fact: According to Plutarch, Cleopatra spoke many languages and was the first of her Greek-Macedonian dynasty to learn Egyptian.

history.q: The Rosetta Stone was found in 1799 during which military campaign?
history.fact: Its 196 BCE decree appears in hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek, which helped Jean-François Champollion decipher hieroglyphs in 1822.

history.q: Which pharaoh fought the Hittites at the Battle of Kadesh around 1274 BCE?
history.fact: A later peace treaty between Ramesses II and the Hittites (c. 1259 BCE) is one of the earliest known; a replica is displayed at the UN in New York.

history.q: Which king is traditionally credited with unifying Upper and Lower Egypt around 3100 BCE?
history.fact: The Narmer Palette shows him wearing the white crown of Upper Egypt on one side and the red crown of Lower Egypt on the other.

history.q: Which female pharaoh of the 18th Dynasty built a terraced mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari?
history.fact: She sent a celebrated trading expedition to the Land of Punt, shown in her temple's reliefs, which brought back incense trees.

history.q: In which year did the Suez Canal open to shipping?
history.fact: The canal has no locks: the Mediterranean and Red Sea are close enough in level that ships sail straight through.

history.q: Pharaoh Akhenaten built a new capital devoted to the sun disc Aten. What was it called?
history.fact: Today called Amarna, the site yielded the 'Amarna letters', diplomatic tablets written in Akkadian cuneiform.

history.q: Which dynasty founded the city of Cairo in 969 CE?
history.fact: The Fatimids also founded Al-Azhar Mosque in 970-972; its university is one of the oldest continuously operating in the world.

technology.q: What writing material did ancient Egyptians make from a reed that grew along the Nile?
technology.fact: The English word 'paper' comes from 'papyrus'. Sheets were made by laying strips of the plant's pith crosswise and pressing them together.

technology.q: Who is credited as the architect of the Step Pyramid of Djoser at Saqqara?
technology.fact: Built around the 27th century BCE, it is one of the oldest large stone buildings; Imhotep was later revered as a god of medicine.

technology.q: How many days were in the ancient Egyptian civil calendar year?
technology.fact: It had 12 months of 30 days plus 5 extra days at year's end, celebrated as the birthdays of gods including Osiris and Isis.

technology.q: Which Egyptian-born scientist won the 1999 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for femtochemistry?
technology.fact: Femtochemistry uses ultrafast laser flashes to watch atoms move during chemical reactions, on timescales of a millionth of a billionth of a second.

technology.q: Which major dam on the Nile, completed in 1970, created Lake Nasser?
technology.fact: Lake Nasser stretches for hundreds of kilometres and crosses into Sudan, where its southern part is called Lake Nubia.

technology.q: Working in Alexandria around 240 BCE, which scholar estimated Earth's circumference by comparing shadows?
technology.fact: He compared the Sun's angle at Syene (modern Aswan) and at Alexandria; his estimate was remarkably close to the true value.

technology.q: What structure did ancient Egyptians use to measure the Nile's flood level?
technology.fact: Flood readings helped officials predict harvests and set taxes. The Nilometer on Cairo's Roda Island dates to 861 CE.

technology.q: During mummification, internal organs were stored in which kind of container?
technology.fact: There were usually four jars, their lids often shaped as the four Sons of Horus, guarding the liver, lungs, stomach and intestines.

technology.q: Which scribe copied the Rhind Mathematical Papyrus around 1550 BCE?
technology.fact: Its 80-plus problems cover fractions, areas and volumes. The papyrus is now held in the British Museum.

technology.q: The Edwin Smith Papyrus is one of the oldest known texts on which subject?
technology.fact: It describes 48 injury cases, each with an examination, diagnosis and treatment, in a remarkably practical style.

art.q: A famous painted limestone bust in Berlin's Neues Museum depicts which queen?
art.fact: Made around 1345 BCE, it was found in 1912 in the Amarna workshop of the sculptor Thutmose.

art.q: Which Egyptian writer won the 1988 Nobel Prize in Literature?
art.fact: He was the first Arabic-language writer to win; his Cairo Trilogy follows one family across three generations.

art.q: The Great Sphinx of Giza has a human head on the body of which animal?
art.fact: It was carved directly from the limestone bedrock of the Giza plateau and is about 73 m long.

art.q: Which collection of spells, written on papyrus and placed in tombs, was meant to guide the dead through the afterlife?
art.fact: Its Egyptian title means roughly 'Book of Coming Forth by Day'. One famous scene shows the heart weighed against the feather of Ma'at.

art.q: Which Egyptian singer was nicknamed 'Kawkab al-Sharq' (Star of the East)?
art.fact: Her monthly live radio concerts drew huge audiences across the Arab world, and a single song could stretch beyond an hour.

art.q: In the 1960s, which organization led the international campaign to relocate the Abu Simbel temples away from rising waters?
art.fact: The temples of Ramesses II were cut into huge blocks and reassembled about 65 m higher, a rescue that inspired the World Heritage system.

art.q: Which Egyptian director made the classic film 'Cairo Station' (1958)?
art.fact: Chahine also starred in the film as a newspaper seller, and received a lifetime achievement prize at Cannes in 1997.

art.q: Egyptian actor Omar Sharif earned an Oscar nomination for which 1962 film?
art.fact: Sharif was also a world-class contract bridge player who wrote newspaper columns about the game.

art.q: Lifelike portraits painted on wooden panels and placed over mummies in Roman-era Egypt are named after which region?
art.fact: Many were painted in encaustic, pigment mixed with hot wax, and they are among the most realistic portraits surviving from antiquity.

art.q: Which Cairo mosque, completed in 879 CE, is known for a minaret with an external spiral staircase?
art.fact: Its founder, Ahmad ibn Tulun, grew up in Samarra, Iraq, and the spiral minaret echoes the famous Great Mosque of Samarra.

politics.q: Which Egyptian president nationalized the Suez Canal in 1956?
politics.fact: He announced the nationalization in a speech in Alexandria on 26 July 1956, sparking the Suez Crisis.

politics.q: Which Egyptian president signed the Camp David Accords with Israel in 1978?
politics.fact: Sadat shared the 1978 Nobel Peace Prize with Israeli Prime Minister Menachem Begin.

politics.q: Who served as Egypt's president from 1981 to 2011?
politics.fact: He stepped down in February 2011 after 18 days of mass protests centred on Cairo's Tahrir Square.

politics.q: Which regional organization was founded in Cairo in 1945 and is headquartered there?
politics.fact: Its headquarters moved to Tunis from 1979 to 1990 before returning to Cairo.

politics.q: Who became Egypt's first president when the republic was declared in 1953?
politics.fact: A leading figure of the 1952 revolution, he was sidelined by Nasser in 1954 and spent years under house arrest.

politics.q: Which Egyptian diplomat served as UN Secretary-General from 1992 to 1996?
politics.fact: He was the first UN Secretary-General from Africa and the Arab world.

politics.q: Which Egyptian diplomat led the International Atomic Energy Agency and shared the 2005 Nobel Peace Prize with it?
politics.fact: He headed the IAEA, the UN's nuclear watchdog based in Vienna, from 1997 to 2009.

politics.q: Which nationalist leader inspired Egypt's 1919 revolution against British rule and later became prime minister?
politics.fact: His exile by the British in 1919 sparked nationwide protests; he led the Wafd Party and became prime minister in 1924.

politics.q: Which ruler took the title King of Egypt when Britain recognized Egyptian independence in 1922?
politics.fact: His son Farouk succeeded him in 1936 and abdicated after the 1952 revolution.

politics.q: Which Ottoman-appointed governor, who took power in 1805, is often called the founder of modern Egypt?
politics.fact: His dynasty ruled Egypt until 1952, and his domed mosque crowns the skyline of Cairo's Citadel.

current-affairs.q: Which container ship blocked the Suez Canal for six days in March 2021?
current-affairs.fact: The 400 m-long ship was freed with help from dredgers, tugs and a high spring tide, while hundreds of vessels queued at each end.

current-affairs.q: Which Egyptian city hosted the COP27 UN climate conference in November 2022?
current-affairs.fact: Delegates agreed to create a 'loss and damage' fund to help vulnerable countries cope with climate impacts.

current-affairs.q: Who won Egypt's presidential election held in December 2023?
current-affairs.fact: It was his third term; 2019 constitutional amendments had extended presidential terms from four years to six.

current-affairs.q: Egyptian forward Mohamed Salah helped which club win the 2024-25 Premier League title?
current-affairs.fact: Salah scored 29 league goals that season, winning the Golden Boot and the Premier League Player of the Season award.

current-affairs.q: In April 2021's 'Pharaohs' Golden Parade', 22 royal mummies were moved to which museum?
current-affairs.fact: The 18 kings and 4 queens, including Ramesses II and Hatshepsut, travelled through Cairo in specially built, shock-absorbing vehicles.

current-affairs.q: In November 2021, Egypt reopened an ancient processional avenue lined with sphinxes linking two temples in which city?
current-affairs.fact: The roughly 2.7 km avenue connects the Karnak and Luxor temples and once hosted processions of the ancient Opet Festival.

current-affairs.q: Egypt became a full member of which group of nations on 1 January 2024?
current-affairs.fact: Egypt joined alongside Ethiopia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates in the group's first expansion since South Africa's entry.

current-affairs.q: In October 2024, the World Health Organization certified Egypt free of which disease?
current-affairs.fact: The WHO noted malaria had been present in Egypt since ancient times; genetic traces of the parasite were found in Tutankhamun's mummy.

current-affairs.q: In 2023, Egypt became the first country to reach WHO 'gold tier' status on the path to eliminating which disease?
current-affairs.fact: Its '100 Million Healthy Lives' campaign, launched in 2018, screened tens of millions of people and offered free treatment.

current-affairs.q: In March 2023, scientists announced a hidden corridor about 9 m long behind the north face of which pyramid?
current-affairs.fact: The ScanPyramids project detected it using muons, particles created by cosmic rays, then confirmed it with an endoscope camera.

general.q: Which river flows north through Egypt to the Mediterranean Sea?
general.fact: Most Egyptians live in the narrow Nile Valley and Delta, a green ribbon covering only a small fraction of the country's land.

general.q: What is the currency of Egypt?
general.fact: The pound is divided into 100 piastres, and Egyptians often call it the 'geneih'.

general.q: Egypt's Sinai Peninsula forms a land bridge between Africa and which continent?
general.fact: At Sinai's southern tip, Ras Mohammed National Park protects some of the Red Sea's most spectacular coral reefs.

general.q: What is the nickname of Egypt's national football team?
general.fact: Egypt has won the Africa Cup of Nations a record seven times, including three in a row from 2006 to 2010.

general.q: Which popular Egyptian street dish combines rice, lentils, pasta and chickpeas topped with tomato sauce and crispy onions?
general.fact: Ta'ameya, Egypt's version of falafel, is traditionally made with fava beans rather than chickpeas.

general.q: Which language, descended from ancient Egyptian, is still used in the liturgy of Egypt's Coptic Church?
general.fact: Coptic is written in an alphabet based on Greek, plus several extra letters borrowed from Demotic Egyptian script.
Rising about 2,629 m in southern Sinai, it stands near St Catherine's Monastery, one of the oldest working Christian monasteries.

general.q: The ancient city of Thebes lies at the site of which modern Egyptian city?
general.fact: Across the Nile on Luxor's West Bank lies the Valley of the Kings, burial ground of New Kingdom pharaohs.

general.q: Which depression in Egypt's Western Desert sinks to about 133 m below sea level?
general.fact: It is one of the lowest points in Africa, and its salt marshes were nearly impassable to armies during World War II.

general.q: Alexander the Great visited a famous oracle at Siwa Oasis dedicated to which god?
general.fact: Many of Siwa's people speak Siwi, a Berber (Amazigh) language, reflecting the oasis's long ties to North Africa's west.
